test_title: RRB Group D Previous Year Paper (Held on: 22 Sept 2022 Shift 2)
subject: general
question:
Which of the following is not a property of ionic compounds?

(i) Ionic compounds have low melting and boiling points.

(ii) Ionic compounds are generally soluble in water and insoluble in solvents like kerosene, petrol, etc.

(iii) Ionic compounds are solids, and to some extent hard, due to the strong force of attraction between positive and negative ions.

(iv) Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state.
solution:
The correct answer is__** i**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **i) Ionic compounds have low melting and boiling points.**

 
 
• This is **not** true.
 
• Ionic compounds generally have **high melting and boiling points** due to the **strong electrostatic forces of attraction** between the positive and negative ions in their lattice structure.
 
• These forces require a significant amount of energy to break.
 
 
 
• **(ii) Ionic compounds are generally soluble in water and insoluble in solvents like kerosene, petrol, etc.**
 
 
• This is **true**.
 
• Ionic compounds are typically soluble in **polar solvents** like water, as water molecules can surround and separate the ions.
 
• They are generally **insoluble in non-polar solvents** like kerosene and petrol, which do not have the ability to break the strong ionic bonds.
 
 
 
• **(iii) Ionic compounds are solids, and to some extent hard, due to the strong force of attraction between positive and negative ions.**
 
 
• This is **true**.
 
• Ionic compounds usually exist as **solids** at room temperature and are **hard** because of the strong ionic bonds that hold the ions in a rigid lattice structure.
 
 
 
• **(iv) Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state.**
 
 
• This is **true**.
 
• In the molten state (or when dissolved in water), ionic compounds dissociate into their respective ions, which are free to move, allowing the compound to **conduct electricity**.
 
 
 
• Hence only statement 1 is not true
